p.src: A density matrix first appears as the natural description of incomplete preparation: a quantum system has been prepared, but we do not know exactly how. Entanglement gives the same mathematical object a deeper role. Even when the state of a composite system is known completely, a subsystem generally has no state vector of its own. Its reduced density matrix contains everything that can be predicted locally. We shall derive that statement in components, test it on two spin states, and use entropy to distinguish product states from entangled ones. Then we shall turn to a second question: how a quantum state changes with time. Preservation of inner products will lead to unitarity, a Hermitian generator, and the Schrödinger equation.

p.src: Density Matrices and Incomplete Preparation

u.src: Density Matrices and Incomplete Preparation
en: Density Matrices and Incomplete Preparation

p.src: Suppose an electron has been placed in a strong magnetic field and allowed to align with it. Someone else chose the field direction and prepared the electron, but did not tell us the direction. The spin may therefore be in a perfectly definite pure state even though we do not know which state it is. We may know a probability distribution over possible preparations, or we may know nothing at all. A density matrix $\rho$ is the quantum description of precisely this kind of incomplete information.

p.src:
The classical analogue is a probability density on phase space or a probability distribution over discrete configurations. The quantum object is an operator with three essential properties: $\rho^\dagger=\rho,
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1,
\qquad
\lambda_i\geq 0,$ where the $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $\rho$. Hermiticity makes the eigenvalues real and supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis. Positivity makes them admissible probabilities, and normalization gives $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i=1.$ In the eigenbasis of $\rho$, $\lambda_i$ is the probability assigned to the $i$-th eigenstate.

p.src: Complete ignorance is the case in which no direction in Hilbert space is preferred: $\rho_{\mathrm{max}}=\frac{1}{n}I.$ Every eigenvalue is $1/n$. At the opposite extreme, complete knowledge is represented by a normalized state $\ket{\psi}$, with $\rho_\psi=\ket{\psi}\bra{\psi}.$ This is the projector onto the one-dimensional subspace spanned by $\ket{\psi}$.

u.src: Entropy as Missing Information
en: Entropy as Missing Information

p.src:
For a classical probability distribution $\{p_i\}$, define $S=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i,$ with $0\log 0$ understood as its limiting value $0$. If one probability equals $1$ and all others vanish, then $S=0$: the state is known. If all $n$ possibilities are equally likely, $p_i=\frac{1}{n},
\qquad
S=-n\left(\frac{1}{n}\log\frac{1}{n}\right)=\log n.$ Thus entropy grows as the probability distribution spreads over more significant possibilities. Roughly, $e^S$ is the effective number of comparably weighted states when natural logarithms are used.

p.src: The contrast with classical mechanics is sharp. Complete classical information about a composite system fixes each of its coordinates and hence each subsystem. A classical probability distribution may certainly be marginalized, but if the original distribution is concentrated at one phase-space point, every marginal is also concentrated at one definite value. Quantum pure states need not have that property.

p.src:
When does $\rho_A$ remain pure? The answer is that the wave function must factorize: $\psi(a,b)=\phi(a)\chi(b).$ Assume $\phi$ and $\chi$ are separately normalized. Substitution into the reduced density matrix gives $\begin{aligned}
\rho_A(a,a')
&=\sum_b\phi(a)\chi(b)\phi^*(a')\chi^*(b) \\
&=\phi(a)\phi^*(a')\sum_b|\chi(b)|^2 \\
&=\phi(a)\phi^*(a').\end{aligned}$ Thus $\rho_A=\ket{\phi}\bra{\phi}.$ It has one eigenvalue $1$, all remaining eigenvalues $0$, and zero entropy.

p.src:
Trace over spin $2$. The diagonal entries are $\begin{aligned}
\rho_1(\uparrow,\uparrow)
&=|\psi(\uparrow,\uparrow)|^2
 +|\psi(\uparrow,\downarrow)|^2
=\frac{1}{2}, \\
\rho_1(\downarrow,\downarrow)
&=|\psi(\downarrow,\uparrow)|^2
 +|\psi(\downarrow,\downarrow)|^2
=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}$ The off-diagonal entry is $\begin{aligned}
\rho_1(\uparrow,\downarrow)
&=\psi(\uparrow,\uparrow)\psi^*(\downarrow,\uparrow)
 +\psi(\uparrow,\downarrow)\psi^*(\downarrow,\downarrow) \\
&=0,\end{aligned}$ and its conjugate also vanishes. Hence $\rho_1
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\frac12&0\\[2pt]
0&\frac12
\end{pmatrix}
=\frac12 I.$

For the $z$-component, $\sigma_3=
\begin{pmatrix}

0&-1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_1\sigma_3)=0.$ For the $x$-component, $\sigma_1=
\begin{pmatrix}

\rho_1\sigma_1

=

\frac12&\frac12\\[2pt]
\frac12&\frac12
\end{pmatrix}, \\
\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_1\sigma_1)&=1.\end{aligned}$

p.src:
The entropy just computed belongs to a subsystem. In the singlet example, $S(\rho_{12})=0,
\qquad
S(\rho_1)=S(\rho_2)=\log 2.$ The whole is pure while each part is mixed. Entanglement entropy therefore does not obey the naive additive rule $S_{12}=S_1+S_2$. For a bipartite pure state the two reduced density matrices have the same nonzero eigenvalues, so their entropies are equal even though the entropy of the whole vanishes.

p.src: Infinitesimal Evolution and the Hamiltonian

u.src: Infinitesimal Evolution and the Hamiltonian
en: Infinitesimal Evolution and the Hamiltonian

p.src:
Let $\epsilon$ be a very small time interval. Since $U(0)=I$, write the first-order expansion $U(\epsilon)=I-i\epsilon h+O(\epsilon^2).$ The minus sign and the factor of $i$ are convenient conventions. Taking the Hermitian conjugate gives $U^\dagger(\epsilon)
=I+i\epsilon h^\dagger+O(\epsilon^2).$ Unitarity then requires $\begin{aligned}
I
&=U^\dagger(\epsilon)U(\epsilon) \\
&=\left(I+i\epsilon h^\dagger\right)
\left(I-i\epsilon h\right)+O(\epsilon^2) \\
&=I+i\epsilon(h^\dagger-h)+O(\epsilon^2).\end{aligned}$ The first-order term must vanish: $\boxed{h^\dagger=h}.$ The infinitesimal generator is Hermitian.

p.src: The Units of Entropy

u.src: The Units of Entropy
en: The Units of Entropy

p.src:
Thermodynamic notation can obscure this point because the Boltzmann constant converts between temperature measured in kelvins and energy: $\expect{K}_{\mathrm{monatomic}}
=\frac32 k_{\mathrm B}T.$ The reversible heat relation is $\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}}=T\,\mathrm dS_{\mathrm{th}}.$ If the information entropy is $S_{\mathrm{info}}=-\sum_i p_i\log p_i,$ then the conventional thermodynamic entropy is $S_{\mathrm{th}}=k_{\mathrm B}S_{\mathrm{info}}.$ Setting $k_{\mathrm B}=1$ measures temperature in energy units and leaves entropy dimensionless. Boltzmann’s constant is then recognized as a conversion factor rather than a new kind of entanglement unit. The historical aside connecting Boltzmann’s statistical ideas with Einstein’s 1905 work on Brownian motion does not alter the information-theoretic definition.
